sent.t: Sachiko-san held my husband's beige fleece sweater to her nose for two seconds, and she said one word.
Three.
Three days.
Hiroshi had worn it three days, and he told me it was still clean.
It looked clean.
It smelled clean to me, because I live in this house, and I smell it every morning.
Sachiko-san does not live in this house, so she smelled the truth.
This is not a video about being dirty.
You are not dirty.
I am not dirty.
It is a video about one small thing, the water that stays in a towel or in a shirt or in a sweater and what happens
in that water while you are sleeping.
Sour is not the smell of sweat.
Sour is the smell of living things that grew after the washing was finished.
By tonight you will know seven rules my mother used and every one of them can be done with what is already in your kitchen and
your laundry room.
No machine to buy.
One thing costs $2, one costs $9, and I will tell you exactly which.
Sour has three ingredients and only three.
Water that stayed too long, oil that never left a fiber, and soap that dried into a film and held the water there.
That is the whole chemistry of it.
When you understand those 3, every rule in this video makes sense, and you will start to see the problem in your own house before you
smell it.
My mother was Fumiko Arai.
She was a kitsukeshi in Jion for 40 years.
She dressed brides and geiko, the women who work in the tea houses, in kimono, by hand, in a room with one window, and a heater
she never turned on.
Every layer of silk had to sit straight, and every layer had to smell of nothing, not perfume, nothing.
I lived 19 years in California, in Sunnyvale, from 1983 to 2002.
My husband worked in an office with carpets and air conditioning, and I learned the American way of washing, everything together, cold water, a big jug
of softener, and a machine that does the work while you sleep.
I did it the American way too.
I am not here to tell you that you are doing it wrong.
I am here to tell you what I changed when I came home and why my towel stopped smelling sour.
Now before the rules, I want you to do one test with me.
It takes one minute and it will tell you more than any video.
Tonight, take a towel from your cupboard, a clean one, the one you think is fine.
Do not smell it in the bathroom where the air is wet.
Take it into the room where you drink your tea, unfold it, fold it again the other way, and put your nose right into the crease
in the middle.
Then tell me what you smell.
If it is nothing, you are lucky.
If it is a little sour, a little like a wet dog, a little like bread that sat too long, that is the smell I am
talking about.
And it did not come from your body.
It came from the last time you washed it.
The test matters.
Smell the towel when it is dry, not when it is wet.
A wet towel always smells of water.
A dry towel tells you what is living inside it.
Rule 1.
Wash towels at 140 degrees Fahrenheit, not cold.
Here is the problem.
The tea oil is not water, it is fat, and fat needs heat to let go of a cotton loop.
When you wash at 68 degrees, the water is comfortable for your hands, and it is also comfortable for the oil.
The oil stays on the fiber.
The towel comes out looking white, feeling clean, and holding a thin film of last week.
My mother washed the white undercollars of the geiko's kimono by hand, in 1975, in a copper basin behind the shop on Hanamikoji.
She used water hot enough that she wore two pairs of gloves, and she changed the water three times.
She told me, cold water is for silk.
Hot water is for skin.
She meant the skin that touches the cloth.
Why does this matter more after 60?
Because we were taught to save.
My generation and yours.
We turned the dial to cold because our mothers did, because energy was expensive, and because cold is gentler on the colors.
For sheets and towels, that is the wrong place to be gentle.
The change.
One load a week.
Towers only.
Hot water.
140 degrees.
Everything else can stay at 86.
If your machine has a sanitized setting, that is fine too, but read the dial and find the temperature in numbers, not pictures.
Rule 2.
The tower comes out of the drum within one hour.
Not two, one.
This is the rule that fixed my house, and it costs nothing.
In 1994, in Sunnyvale, my friend Carol Whitfield, she is 70 now and lives in Sacramento, had a machine in a little room off the kitchen.
She started the load before bed and took it out in the morning.
Her towels were always a little sour.
She blamed the water.
She bought a new machine.
The new machine did the same thing, because the machine was never the problem.
The towers sat in a warm, wet drum for nine hours, and that drum was a small greenhouse.
After the wash, a tower is clean and wet, and it is also warm, and the door is closed.
Bacteria do not need much.
They need water, warmth, and one night.
The change.
When the machine stops, the towers go out.
If you cannot hang them right away, Run the rings and spin again, but do not leave them in a bowl.
In the rainy season here, in June, I hang them inside, in the room with the fan, and they dry in four hours.
The fan costs less than a coffee.
And for us, after 60, there is one more thing about this rule.
We have a favorite towel.
We use it after the shower, we hang it on the rail, and at 8 in the evening it is still a little damp in the
middle, so we use it again in the morning.
A towel that never fully dries is never really clean, even if it was washed on Sunday.
Two towels used on alternate days dry completely, and that costs nothing at all.
Rule 3.
Use one third of the soap you are using now.
I know how this sounds.
More soap should be cleaner.
It is not.
The machine uses the same amount of water, and the extra soap has nowhere to go.
It stays in the folds, in the hem, in the thick part of the towel, where the loop is doubled.
Then it dries into a film, and the film holds water, and the water holds the smell.
Mr.
Okada sells linen and tenugi in the Nishiki market.
He has a store about two meters wide, with a wooden counter his father built.
He keeps the ends of the bolts for me, the last half meter of linen, the cotton with the long dye.
One afternoon I told him my kitchen clothes smelled sour even after washing.
He picked one up, rubbed it between his fingers, and said, Too much soap.
It is not dirty.
It is sticky.
For us, after 60, there is a second reason.
Our skin is drier, so we use more cream.
And the cream goes onto the towel.
And the cream is oil.
Oil plus too much soap makes a film that never rinses out.
The change.
Fill the cup one third.
If your load is small, half of that.
And once a month, run the towers with no soap at all and a cup of white vinegar in the rinse.
That is the reset.
Rule 4.
The machine has a rubber lip and it is the dirtiest thing in your house.
I did not know this for years.
Open the door of a front-loading machine and pull the rubber gasket back all the way around, especially at the bottom.
There is a grey film in there.
That film is the same sour smell, concentrated.
My granddaughter Yui moved into a small apartment in Osaka in 2023 and called me because her clothes smelled after washing.
She is 22.
She is careful.
She cleaned everything.
She had never looked at the gasket.
We cleaned it with a toothbrush nobody uses and a cup of white vinegar and the black water that came out made her laugh and then
made her quiet.
The change.
Once a month, a toothbrush and vinegar.
Two dollars.
Leave the door open when the machine is empty.
Always.
And leave the soap drawer out to dry once a week.
Older machines are worse for this.
The rubber hardens, it does not close tight, and a little water stays in the fold all week.
You do not need a new machine.
You need 10 minutes a month and a chair to sit on, because bending down is the hard part, not the cleaning.
Rule 5.
No softener on towels.
Vinegar instead.
Softener is made to coat fiber.
That is what soft is, a thin layer.
On a towel, that layer does two things.
It stops the towel from taking water, and it traps the oil underneath it.
Your towel feels lovely and dries nothing, and after a month, it smells sour even though it is clean.
I bought a big jug of softener in Sunnyvale, the kind that lasts a year.
In 2002, when we came back to Kyoto, I put it in the cupboard under the sink and did not use it.
In 2003, I threw it away, and I did not buy another one for 20 years.
After 60, we like soft things.
The skin is thinner, the cotton feels rough, and the softener feels kind.
I understand this very well, but a towel is a tool before it is a comfort.
Keep the softener for a sweater if you must, not for the towel that touches your face.
The change, half a cup of plain white vinegar where the softener goes.
It costs about $2 a bottle, and it does not smell of vinegar when it dries.
It disappears, it takes the soap film out and the towel comes out soft because it is actually clean.
And while we are in the kitchen, the dishcloth is the worst offender in the house.
It touches everything, it stays wet on the counter and then it goes into the machine with the bath towels.
I wash them separately in the hottest load and I change them every day.
A pack of 10 plain cotton cloths is $9 at the market, and that is the $9 I told you about at the beginning.
It is the best money in this whole video.
Rule 6.
One hour of morning sun, then shade.
This is the oldest rule in this house, and it is free.
My mother put everything on the balcony before 10 in the morning, not at noon, not in the afternoon, before 10.
She said, the morning sun is clean and the afternoon sun is tired.
I do not know if that is science.
I know that the sun before noon comes in at a low angle under the roof of the balcony, and it is strong enough to kill
what grew in the wash, and it is not strong enough to fade the colors because the cloth is not in the direct heat for long.
In June, when it rains for three weeks, there is no sun.
Then I use the fan and I turn the towels over after two hours.
The rule is the same.
Moving air and time.
The change.
One hour in the morning sun, then move the towels to the shade.
Do not leave wool in the sun.
Wool goes into the shade from the first minute, and in winter, when it is 35 degrees inside this wooden house, the sun through the window
is still warm enough for cotton.
I put the towels out at nine and bring them in at eleven, because cold air with sun dries cotton better than warm air in a
closed room.
Mrs.
Kinoshita, my neighbor across the street, walks the Philosopher's Path every morning.
10,000 steps, she says, and she says the same thing about her shoes that I say about towels.
Air them, do not bake them.
She is 81 and she has been right about most things for 50 years.
Before the last rule, one small thing.
If you have watched this far, you are the kind of person who smells the towel.
Please press the like button and subscribe.
It helps this small channel more than you know, and every Sunday, Yui reads me the comments with my tea.
Rule 7.
And this is the one nobody in America talks about.
Synthetic fabric keeps oil, not water, oil.
A cotton towel releases the oil into hot water.
A polyester fleece holds it, because polyester is plastic, and oil likes plastic.
That is why Hiroshi's beige fleece, washed and clean, still said three days to Sachiko-san.
The change for tonight is small.
After he wears it, it goes on the balcony for one hour, in the air, inside out.
That is not the full fix.
The full fix is my mother's wash for wool and fleece, which is a different method, with a different temperature and a different soap.
and I will show you that another time because it deserves its own video.
Now the check for tonight.
Take the towel, the one you smelled in the crease.
Look at the label.
Put it in a hot wash with a third of the soap and half a cup of vinegar.
Hang it outside before 10 tomorrow morning for one hour.
Then smell the crease again in the dry room and tell me in the comments what you found, not what you read, what you smelled.
My mother said, your clothes speak before you do, so be careful what they say.
A towel is the first thing that touches your face in the morning.
It should say nothing.
And one more thing, because Karo called me on Sunday, and she was wearing what she always wears, jeans.
She said, Michiko, I live in jeans.
What do I wear on the plane?
I will answer that next week, because there is a Kyoto way to wear jeans at our age, and it is not what you think.
If you only do one thing tonight, do the test, take the towel, smell the crease, and trust your nose.
Everything else in this video will follow from that one minute.
Thank you for being here.
Tell me about your towel.
